What are the best paper planners for ADHD adults?

Paper wins when your phone is the problem. A single-purpose planner has no notifications, and writing by hand can make a plan feel more committed.

Look for undated pages, so a skipped week doesn't leave a trail of blank days, and one spread that shows the week and today together. Here's how six popular paper options compare.

Prices from each maker's own website on October 20, 2026. Paper planner prices change often, so check before you buy.

Planner Pads - best for seeing the whole week at once

Planner Pads uses a "funnel" spread: categories at the top, the day's priorities in the middle and appointments at the bottom, with all seven days on two pages. The ADHD organization ADDA has reviewed it for ADHD adults.

It suits people who lose track of anything they can't see. It's dated, so a missed month still shows.

Laurel Denise - best for visual learners who like paper

Laurel Denise planners show the week and the day on the same spread, so you get context and focus together. The premium price is real, so it fits people who already know they stick with paper.

Happy Planner - best for customizers who love stickers

Happy Planner is a disc-bound system you can rearrange, with a large sticker and insert range. Decorating can be the reason you open it, but it can also turn into its own way of avoiding the plan.

Panda Planner - best for a guided daily page

Panda Planner gives each day a fixed structure, which removes the blank-page problem. The undated 3-month daily version is a low-risk way to test whether paper sticks for you.

Clever Fox - best for goals plus a weekly plan

Clever Fox's undated planner pairs goal pages with weekly and monthly views. It's sold mainly through retailers, so the price moves around.

Bullet Journal - best for high-novelty seekers

The Bullet Journal method works in any notebook, and you draw your own layouts, called spreads. That flexibility keeps it fresh, but the planner is only as good as your last spread.

If you've abandoned a bullet journal before, a simpler system may stick better.

Panda Planner - best for a guided daily page

Panda Planner Classic gives each day a fixed structure: a morning review, a schedule, top priorities and an end-of-day review. It is undated, 5.25 x 8.25 inches, and lasts 3 months, which makes it a low-risk test of whether paper sticks.

Happy Planner - best for customizers who love stickers

Happy Planner is disc-bound, so you can add, remove and move pages. Decorating can be the reason you open it, but it can also turn into its own way of avoiding the plan.

Bullet Journal - best for high-novelty seekers

The Bullet Journal method works in any notebook, and you draw your own layouts, called spreads. The official Leuchtturm1917 Edition 2 notebook has 206 numbered dot-grid pages and a short guide in the back pocket.

That flexibility keeps it fresh, but the planner is only as good as your last spread. If you've abandoned a bullet journal before, a simpler system may stick better.

Planner Pads - best for seeing the whole week at once

Planner Pads uses a "funnel" spread: tasks by category at the top, each day's priorities in the middle and appointments at the bottom. The ADHD organization ADDA reviewed it and says the funnel gives adults with ADHD outside structure for sorting and prioritizing.

Clever Fox - best for goals plus a weekly plan

The Clever Fox Planner PRO is undated and 8.5 x 11 inches, with 12 monthly pages up front and 52 weekly pages after them. Goal pages connect what you want this year to what you do this week.

Laurel Denise - best for visual learners who like paper

Laurel Denise planners show the week and the day on the same spread, so you get context and focus together. Most editions are dated, and the premium price fits people who already know they stick with paper.
